Project overview

A platform connecting veterinary clinics with specialist consultants — primarily radiologists — for remote case review and diagnostic reporting. Designed to replace a patchwork of outdated tools and Jira boards with a purpose-built, role-specific workflow.

A time-boxed PoC delivered in 6 weeks with strictly limited access to requirements. The challenge: design a credible, production-ready product from almost nothing — and convince the client we were the right team to build it.

The context

Design under pressure.

The potential client gave us a fixed window to demonstrate what we were capable of. We had minimal documentation, no direct access to end users, and a product scope that was intentionally left vague. The goal wasn't to design a perfect product — it was to show we could navigate ambiguity and deliver something compelling fast.

01 — Understanding

Product
Definition

The client — a company operating in veterinary teleradiology — needed a platform to streamline how clinics send imaging cases to specialist radiologists for remote review. Their current setup involved an outdated third-party application supplemented by Jira boards to track cases, communicate, and manage assignments.

The brief we received was intentionally minimal. We understood the core concept: an intermediary platform between veterinary clinics (who submit cases) and specialists (who review them). Beyond that, we had to make informed assumptions — and make them quickly.

The problem
Outdated, fragmented tools

The client relied on an aging application paired with Jira boards — two separate systems creating manual overhead and friction for every user role.

The goal
A unified, purpose-built platform

One application designed around the actual workflows of clinics, radiologists, and case managers — with role-specific views and a submission flow built from scratch.

Our objective
Prove we could deliver

The PoC wasn't about shipping a finished product — it was about demonstrating design capability and the ability to make confident decisions without perfect information.

Key insight

"The biggest risk wasn't technical. It was emotional — users who had worked with the same tools for years would need convincing that something new was worth the switch."

User roles

Three distinct users.
One platform.

🏥
Role 01
Veterinary Clinic
The submitter. Creates new cases by providing patient details and uploading DICOM imaging files.
  • Search for or add new patients
  • Upload DICOM zip files
  • Set modality type, body area, turnaround
  • Track case progress and reports
🔬
Role 02
Radiologist / Specialist
The reviewer. Works through an assigned queue of cases, filtering by status, modality, and urgency.
  • View all assigned and unassigned cases
  • Filter by status, species, modality
  • Access case details and DICOM files
  • Write and submit diagnostic reports
📋
Role 03
Case Manager
The coordinator. Broadest view — oversees all cases across clinics and specialists, manages assignments.
  • View all cases across the platform
  • Assign unassigned cases to specialists
  • Monitor SLAs and turnaround compliance
  • Access complete case history and edits
Design constraints

Designing
in the dark.

01
Very limited time
Six weeks from kickoff to deliverable. We defaulted to Mantine — a React component library — to eliminate low-value decisions and stay focused on UX logic.
02
Minimal requirements documentation
No user stories, no detailed specs. We had to infer requirements from the product category, the client's existing workflow, and logical user needs — and document our assumptions as we went.
03
High user attachment to existing processes
Users had worked with the same tools for years. We had to design something familiar enough not to frighten, but clearly better.
04
No direct user access
No user interviews, no surveys, no shadowing. We leaned on domain knowledge — the clinical workflow context, DICOM imaging specifics, and the pressures each role operates under.
02 — Design

Decisions
made.

Without the luxury of iteration cycles, every design decision had to be intentional and defensible. We focused our effort on three areas: the case submission flow, the role-differentiated case list, and the case detail view with audit history.

Using Mantine's component library allowed us to work at the UX level — concentrating on information architecture, interaction logic, and hierarchy — without reinventing primitives.

Submission flow
3-step case creation wizard

Patient Details → Case Details → Review Case. This reduced cognitive load for clinic staff who submit many cases per day, and made it clear where they were in the process.

Information architecture
Role-specific views from the start

Same data, different filters, different columns — designed around what each user actually needs to do their job, not a single shared view with access restrictions bolted on.

Status system
Clear, colour-coded case states

To Report, In Progress, Final, To Assign, On Hold — colour-coded and visible at every layer. An at-a-glance system that doesn't require reading every row.

Audit & transparency
Case history as a trust mechanism

Every edit, field change, and timestamp logged and visible as a side panel. In a clinical context, this wasn't a nice-to-have — it was a signal the platform could be trusted.

03 — Outcome

The work
itself.

Eight screens delivered across the PoC — covering the end-to-end submission flow, the role-specific case list views, and the case detail with audit history. Each screen was designed with production intent: Mantine components, consistent spacing and hierarchy, role-specific contextual decisions throughout.

Case creation flow — clinic view

Step 1 — Patient Details. Search for existing patient or add new. Consultation type sets context for the whole case.

Step 2 — Case Details. DICOM upload, modality type, body area, clinical history, and turnaround priority.

Case detail — patient view & audit history

Case detail — patient information, case ID, speciality tag. Scannable layout for quick reference during review.

Case history panel — every edit logged with timestamp, user, field changed, and old vs new value.

Case list — role-specific views

Clinic view — creation date, progress, status, case ID, patient data. Colour-coded status badges.

Radiologist view — All Cases / Assigned to Me / Unassigned. Due date as primary sort. Last comment preview.

Radiologist view filtered — Status: To Report active. Filter chip shown inline; Clear All available.

Case Manager view — broadest columns: creation date, due date, status, assignee, speciality, modality.

Reflection

What I learned.

What worked
Making decisions visible
  • Designing role-specific views from day one forced clarity on information hierarchy and prevented feature creep.
  • Using Mantine as a base kept delivery fast without sacrificing quality — component decisions made once, applied consistently.
  • Prioritising the audit trail early signalled trustworthiness to the client. A platform that logs everything is one people can rely on.
  • The 3-step wizard reduced scope ambiguity: once we had the steps, the fields fell into place naturally.
What I'd do differently
More time on edge cases
  • I'd have pushed harder on DICOM upload edge cases — what happens when a file is corrupted, or the folder structure is wrong?
  • Turnaround options like "Out of Hours Urgent" vs "Out of Hours Priority" needed better microcopy — the labels weren't self-explanatory.
  • Even 3 guerrilla interviews with vets or radiologists would have replaced weeks of assumption-making. A PoC benefits from any real user grounding.
A credible, production-intent PoC — delivered in 6 weeks.
The Vet App PoC demonstrated that complex, multi-role B2B products can be designed strategically under tight constraints. By focusing on role clarity, workflow logic, and visual consistency — rather than chasing completeness — we delivered something that felt real, not rushed. The constraints were the design brief.
